## 1.  ARIMA vs. ETS

#2.1 — Data and Plots

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN   = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date),
            sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)

liquor |>
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(title = "Monthly U.S. Retail Sales: Beer, Wine & Liquor Stores",
       x = NULL, y = "Sales (millions of dollars)")

liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Plot of Log Liquor Sales (1992–2019)",
       x = NULL, y = "log(Sales)")
```

Trend:\
The series exhibits a clear and persistent upward trend over the sample period. This is visible in the seasonal plot as the year-lines progress from the bottom (orange/red, early 1990s, log(sales) ≈ 7.2–7.5) to the top (pink/magenta, late 2010s, log(sales) ≈ 8.3–8.7), reflecting steady growth in liquor store sales over nearly three decades.

Seasonal Pattern:\
The within-year seasonal pattern is very consistent across all years. January and February are the lowest months, forming a clear trough at the start of each year. Sales then gradually rise through spring and summer, with a mild secondary peak around May–July. There is a modest dip in September, followed by a sharp and dramatic surge in December, which is by far the highest month of the year.

Do Seasonal Swings Grow with the Level?\
Yes. In the raw (level) sales data, the absolute size of the December spike grows larger as overall sales rise over time, which is multiplicative seasonality. However, in the log seasonal plot shown, the year-lines are roughly parallel, indicating that the seasonal amplitude is approximately constant in percentage terms across years.

\### 2.2 — Model Specifications

```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()
liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

Chosen specifications: \
ARIMA selected: ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)\[12\] with drift;

ETS selected: ETS(A,A,A).

ARIMA differencing: With d = 0 and D = 1, the model applies one seasonal difference (lag 12) but no regular differencing. The series is stationary after removing the seasonal unit root, requiring no further differencing.

ETS(A,A,A): Additive errors, additive trend (the level grows linearly over time), and additive seasonal component (seasonal effects enter additively and are constant in size).

#2.2b — Residual Diagnostics

```{r}
# dof = p + q + P + Q = 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```

The residuals do not pass the white noise test. Several ACF autocorrelations exceed the confidence bands, particularly at lags 7–8, 11–12, and especially lag 24 (≈ 0.28). The Ljung–Box test (statistic ≈ 120, p ≈ 0) strongly rejects white noise at any conventional level. As noted in the problem set, however, this tells us there may be structure left to capture, not that the model will forecast poorly.

#2.3 — The Horse Race

```{r}
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")
```

#2.3a. How many different forecast origins will be considered in this TS-CV?

The TS-CV uses an initial training sample of 120 months (January 1992 – December 2001), then expands by one month at a time through the end of the sample. Since there are 336 total observations and the final training sample is dropped (as we cannot observe what it would forecast), there are 216 forecast origins, with the first one-month-ahead forecast targeting January 2002 and the last targeting December 2019.

2.3b.

What are the dates of the first and last forecasts?

**Dates of the first and last forecasts:**

**First forecast =** January 2002

**Last forecast =** December 2019

Which model forecasts most accurately? Do the two metrics agree?

```{r}
liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |> forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Model", "RMSE", "MAE"),
               caption   = "Table 1: One-Month-Ahead Forecast Accuracy (TS-CV, Jan 2002–Dec 2019)")
```

ARIMA is the most accurate model by a clear margin under both metrics, it achieves an RMSE of 81.4 and an MAE of 65.7, compared to 94.4 / 72.3 for ETS and 161 / 137 for the seasonal naïve benchmark. Yes, the two metrics agree: ARIMA ranks first, ETS second, and the seasonal naïve last under both RMSE and MAE. The seasonal naïve benchmark performs substantially worse, confirming that the parametric models add meaningful value over the simple benchmark.

2.4

Report both DM statistics and p-values. In two or three sentences: what do you conclude? If you were the liquor store chain, which model would you use?

```{r}
liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales), by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

# ARIMA vs. ETS
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets,    h = 1, power = 2)

# ARIMA vs. Seasonal Naïve
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)
```

ARIMA vs. ETS: DM = −2.906, p-value = 0.0040

ARIMA vs. Seasonal Naïve: DM = −10.755, p-value \< 2.2e-16

Both Diebold-Mariano tests reject the null hypothesis of equal forecast accuracy at conventional significance levels. The negative DM statistics in both tests confirm that ARIMA generates systematically smaller squared errors than ETS (DM = −2.91, p = 0.004) and dramatically smaller errors than the seasonal naïve benchmark (DM = −10.76, p \< 2.2e-16), meaning ARIMA's accuracy advantage is statistically significant in both cases. If I were the liquor store chain, I would use **ARIMA**: it is statistically and meaningfully more accurate than both competitors, and the overwhelming rejection against the seasonal naïve benchmark gives strong confidence that the model is capturing genuine structure in the data beyond a simple seasonal pattern.

## 2.  Forecast Combination

3a

Report the results in a table. How does combo compare to each of the models that go into it?

```{r}
liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  select(.model, RMSE, MAE) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Model", "RMSE", "MAE"),
               caption   = "Table 2: One-Month-Ahead Accuracy Including Equal-Weight Combination")
```

The equal-weight combination does not beat the best individual model. With an RMSE of 85.19 and MAE of 66.77, combo sits between its two components: it outperforms ETS (RMSE: 94.35, MAE: 72.31) but falls short of ARIMA alone (RMSE: 81.43, MAE: 65.65). Both metrics agree on this ranking. This outcome illustrates the forecast combination puzzle, while combining forecasts typically reduces error relative to any single model, that benefit requires the component models to make meaningfully different mistakes. Here, averaging in a clearly weaker model (ETS) only dilutes the stronger one (ARIMA), producing a combined forecast that improves on the worst but cannot surpass the best.

3b

Based on this correlation, and on the DM test in 2.4, explain in two or three sentences why the combination did or did not beat the best individual model.

```{r}
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```

The combination failed to beat ARIMA because the two conditions that make combining most beneficial were both absent here. The ARIMA and ETS forecast errors are very highly correlated (r = 0.879), meaning the two models make nearly identical mistakes. Moreover, the DM test (p = 0.004) confirmed that ARIMA is statistically significantly more accurate than ETS, so including ETS in the average only drags the stronger model down rather than complementing it.

## 3. VAR vs. BVAR.

```{r}

qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))

growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y       <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
N       <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual  <- y[121:N, ]
```

4.2

Which VAR forecasts better? For how many of the eight variables? Given that the VAR(4) contains the VAR(1) as a special case, why might the smaller model forecast better?

```{r}

var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)
  M <- ncol(z)
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rbind(`VAR(1)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var1),
      `VAR(4)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var4)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Table 3: OLS VAR RMSE by Variable")
```

The VAR(1) forecasts better for all 8 variables. Its RMSE is lower across the board.

Although the VAR(4) nests the VAR(1) as a special case, the extra lags add many more parameters to estimate (the PS notes a VAR(4) with 8 variables has 264 coefficients). With a limited training sample, OLS overfits the extra parameters to noise, increasing estimation error out of sample, which is exactly the bias-variance tradeoff described in the lecture slides.

4.3b

```{r}
fc_bvar_03  <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")
var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")

var_results |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Table 4: RMSE by Variable and Model")
```

How does the BVAR(4) with \\(\\lambda = 0.3\\) compare to the OLS VAR(4)? Both have the same variables and the same lags, so what explains any difference?

Ans:\
The BVAR beats the OLS VAR(4) for all 8 variables. Both models use identical variables and lags, so the difference is entirely due to shrinkage: the Minnesota prior pulls the 264 OLS coefficients toward zero, reducing the overfitting that makes the OLS VAR(4) worse than even the VAR(1)

How does it compare to the VAR(1)?

Ans:

Results are mixed — the VAR(1) still beats the BVAR(4) for most variables (gdp, cons, emp, unrate, ffr). The BVAR wins only for inv, infl, and gs10. λ=0.3 provides moderate shrinkage but not enough to consistently beat the more parsimonious VAR(1).

What happens when \\(\\lambda = 0.05\\)? What does this tell you about the amount of shrinkage? Suppose you used this table to choose your forecasting model. Would the winner’s RMSE here be a fair estimate of how accurately it will forecast in the future? Why or why not?

Ans:\
λ=0.05: Performance deteriorates badly for most variables (e.g., infl jumps from 0.197 to 0.330, emp from 0.211 to 0.315). This tells us λ=0.05 is too tight, it over-shrinks the coefficients toward zero, creating too much approximation error that outweighs the reduction in estimation error.

Is the winner's RMSE a fair estimate? No. We selected the best model by looking at all four RMSEs computed over the same evaluation sample, so the winner's RMSE is optimistically biased, a form of overfitting the model selection to the data.

**4.3c.** For GDP growth, test whether the VAR(4) and the BVAR(4) with \\(\\lambda = 0.3\\) are equally accurate, using a Diebold–Mariano test with squared error loss. Then write the code to repeat the test for a second variable of your choice (i.e. not GDP growth). What do you conclude? How does this affect how you think about your results in 4.3b?

```{r}
# GDP: VAR(4) vs. BVAR(4)
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]
forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

# Consumption: VAR(4) vs. BVAR(4)
e_var4_cons <- actual[, "cons"] - fc_var4[, 2]
e_bvar_cons <- actual[, "cons"] - fc_bvar_03[, 2]
forecast::dm.test(e_var4_cons, e_bvar_cons, h = 1, power = 2)
```

**Conclusion:**

For GDP, DM = 2.14 (p = 0.035), rejecting equal accuracy at the 5% level, the BVAR(4) is statistically significantly more accurate than the OLS VAR(4).

**Effect on 4.3b:** This strengthens confidence that the BVAR's lower RMSE for GDP in 4.3b reflects a genuine improvement from shrinkage, not just sampling noise. However, variables where the RMSE gap was smaller (e.g., cons, ffr) may not show statistically significant differences, so the table-level RMSE comparisons in 4.3b should be interpreted cautiously variable-by-variable.

## 4.  Factor Model.

5.1c

```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode  <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md     <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,
         "2" = d(x),
         "3" = d(d(x)),
         "4" = log(x),
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm_dates <- as.Date(md[["sasdate"]], "%m/%d/%Y")

fm <- bind_cols(map2(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series)) |>
  mutate(date = fm_dates, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]
dim(fm)
```

5.1C

The codes from the data are: INDPRO = 5, PAYEMS = 5, CPIAUCSL = 6, FEDFUNDS = 2.

INDPRO (code 5): transformed as the monthly growth rate (100 × Δlog), since it is a quantity index whose natural unit of change is percent growth.

PAYEMS (code 5): transformed as the monthly growth rate, since it is an employment level and percent change is the natural measure.

CPIAUCSL (code 6): transformed as the change in the monthly inflation rate (100 × Δ²log), capturing how inflation itself is accelerating or decelerating.

FEDFUNDS (code 2): transformed as the first difference in percentage points, since it is already expressed as a percent and its natural change unit is percentage-point moves.

Why FEDFUNDS differs from INDPRO: INDPRO is a quantity index (bounded well above zero), so log-growth rates are well-defined and economically meaningful; FEDFUNDS is an interest rate already in percent, so percentage-point changes are the natural transformation, and log growth rates would be undefined or nonsensical when rates approach zero.

5.2a

What share of the variation in all 121 series do the first three factors explain? This should match the result we saw in class.

```{r}
Z  <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()
pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```

Ans:

The first three factors explain **29.45%** of the variation in all 121 series (Cumulative Proportion = 0.29453 for PC3). This matches the result shown in class.

5.2c

The names of the series can be looked up in the FRED-MD documentation, FRED-MD_updated_appendix.pdf, which is posted on Canvas. Based on these series, and on your plot, how would you describe what each factor captures?

```{r}
F1 <- pc$x[, 1] * sign(cor(pc$x[, 1], fm$INDPRO))

tibble(date = fm$date, F1 = F1) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, F1)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "First Factor from FRED-MD", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 1], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
sort(abs(cor(pc$x[, 2], Z))[1, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:8]
```

Ans:

**Factor 1** is a **real activity factor**. Its top correlated series are all employment and industrial production measures (PAYEMS, IPMANSICS, USGOOD, INDPRO, MANEMP, etc.), and the plot shows sharp drops at every recession.

**Factor 2** is an **inflation factor**. Its top correlated series are almost entirely price indices (CUSR0000SAC, CPIAUCSL, DNDGRG3M086SBEA, PCEPI, CPIULFSL, etc.), consistent with the lecture's finding of a correlation of 0.72 with CPI inflation.

**5.3. Replicate the Horse Race from Class**

In class we saw an RMSE of 0.617 for the AR(1) and 0.589 with the factors. Confirm that you get the same numbers. Why would it be cheating to estimate the factors once, using the full sample, and use those in the horse race?

```{r}
#| cache: true
ip   <- fm$INDPRO
n    <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T  <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]
  d_df <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new  <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y,  d_df), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d_df), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```

Ans:\
Estimating factors once on the full sample would give each forecast origin T access to future data (T+1 through n) embedded in the factors. This is look-ahead bias. The forecast at origin T would use information that wasn't available until after T, artificially inflating the apparent accuracy of the factor model.

5.4

Do the factors improve the forecast of 12-month CPI inflation? By what percentage do they reduce the RMSE? Is the difference statistically significant?

```{r}
#| cache: true
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g     = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)
  g  <- lv$g
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T  <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i    <- 1:(T - h)
    d    <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new  <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series,
         forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR   = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)),
         RMSE_FA   = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR    = mean(abs(e_ar)),
         MAE_FA    = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL") |> knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

Ans:

Yes, the factors improve the 12-month CPI inflation forecast. They reduce the RMSE by approximately **10.4%** (from 2.11 to 1.89). The DM p-value of **0.000443** indicates the difference **is** statistically significant at conventional levels.

## 5.  Reflection.

Across this problem set, the same theme emerged in every horse race: simple, parsimonious models are surprisingly hard to beat through brute-force estimation, but beatable through targeted regularization. In the liquor store horse race, ARIMA beat ETS, yet combining them added almost nothing because their errors were nearly identical (r = 0.879).This diversification only helps when models make different mistakes. In the VAR analysis, the unrestricted VAR(4) was actually beaten by its own nested special case, VAR(1), because fitting 264 coefficients from a limited sample causes overfitting; the BVAR's Minnesota prior corrected this by shrinking coefficients toward zero, recovering most of the lost performance. The factor model showed the same logic in a different guise: instead of estimating hundreds of free parameters, factors compress 121 series into just three numbers, discarding noise and retaining only the common variation that is likely to be informative out-of-sample. At their core, shrinkage (BVAR), equal-weight averaging (forecast combination), and dimensionality reduction (factors) are all expressions of the same idea.
